newsitem.title: USA: Report shows funding gaps between school districts.
newsitem.headline: Report shows funding gaps between school districts.

text.p: A funding gap between wealthy and poor school districts exists in 37 states despite federal and state efforts to equalize funding, according to a General Accounting Office report released Monday.

The report, requested by Senators Jeff Bingaman, D-N.M., Christopher Dodd, D-Conn., and Carol Mosely-Braun, D-Ill., indicated that wealthy districts on average spent 24 percent more per student than poor districts.
Meanwhile, poor districts in 35 states made a greater tax effort than wealthy districts.

The study also tracked states' share of school funding. In the 1991-92 school year, state funding ranged from a low of eight percent in New Hampshire to 85 percent in Massachusetts and nearly 98 percent in Hawaii.
An analysis of how equitably those dollars were distributed found Nevada ranking first in equalization effort, while New Hampshire ranked last.

Arkansas, Kentucky, Florida and New Mexico also received high rankings behind Nevada, while South Dakota, Oregon, Massachusetts and Illinois were in the lowest five rankings before New Hampshire, according to the report.
"The states are not making enough progress toward equalizing education funds, which highlights the need to continue strong federal support for education," Bingaman said in a news release.

Mosley-Braun added the study underscores the need for more federal funding. She has proposed legislation that would provide $5 billion to help states and local school districts repair school buildings.
